Assignment 06 / Sculpting for Design

Essence in Subtraction

Growth and blooming, discovered by carving an abstract rose from floral foam.

Floral foam · Carving

This foam study explores subtraction as a way of finding form. Unlike additive sculpting, a carved-away element cannot simply be put back. Medha began with an idea of growth and allowed the rose to emerge as she worked.

01

Something growing from a block

The foam exercise called for an abstract form. Medha began without a fixed design, but wanted the piece to suggest growth or blooming. As she carved, that idea became an abstract rose with vine-like forms spreading out from the bud.

She enjoyed the way her visualisation gradually took shape as more material was removed. The finished form holds a contrast between the curled, enclosed centre and the lower forms extending out around it.

02

A form discovered through subtraction

The assignment called for something abstract, so Medha did not begin with a fixed design. Her aim was to suggest growth or blooming. The curled bud and spreading, vine-like forms developed through the act of removing material.

The different photographs record the same sculpture from several viewpoints. The central spiral and surrounding openings become more apparent as the object is turned, while the broad base connects the smaller curves into one form.

03

Working with floral foam

Medha describes the foam as pleasant to work with and says she enjoyed seeing her visualisation slowly materialise. The process was a gradual negotiation between the idea she had in mind and the shape left after each cut.

Her reflection also identifies the defining challenge of subtraction: its permanence. The finished rose records a sequence of decisions made by taking material away.

The original pages.

This shared submission documents the foam study on page 2 and the separate plaster carvings on pages 3–4.
